name: Genghis Khan
info: Genghis Khan (born Temüjin; c. 1162 – 1227) was the founder and first khan of the Mongol Empire, who united the Mongol tribes by 1206 and then conquered large parts of China and Central Asia.

facts.born: c. 1162 (historians also favour 1155 or 1167), at Delüün Boldog on the Onon River according to the Secret History of the Mongols; eldest child of Yesügei, a chieftain of the Borjigin clan, and Hö'elün
facts.died: 18 or 25 August 1227, during the siege of the Western Xia capital Zhongxing, after months of illness following a fall from his horse; the exact cause is disputed
facts.role: Khan of the Mongols (acclaimed by his followers before c. 1187); Genghis Khan, first khan of the Mongol Empire, 1206–1227
facts.known: Uniting the tribes of the Mongolian steppe; founding the Mongol Empire; reorganising Mongol society into a decimal military system; the conquest of the Jin capital Zhongdu; the destruction of the Khwarazmian Empire; campaigns that killed millions; a trading system spanning Eurasia

t: Abandoned by his father's people as a child, Temüjin built a following through personal loyalty and alliances and by 1204 had defeated every rival on the Mongolian steppe.
As Genghis Khan from 1206 he replaced tribal loyalties with a decimal military system and commanders chosen for merit, bound to the khan and his family.
His campaigns against the Western Xia, the Jin and the Khwarazmian Empire killed millions and devastated China, Central Asia and Persia, while opening trade and exchange across Eurasia.
dyk: The Secret History of the Mongols, the main source for his youth, is often critical of its subject: it presents Genghis Khan as indecisive and as having a phobia of dogs, and it records that he killed his own half-brother.
ev: Temüjin is born to the Borjigin chieftain Yesügei and his wife Hö'elün; the year is disputed
He is defeated by his former sworn brother Jamukha at Dalan Baljut
He joins a Jin campaign against the Tatars and helps Toghrul to regain the lordship of the Kereit
Attacked by Toghrul and defeated at Qalaqaljid Sands, he regroups at Baljuna and overpowers the Kereit
An assembly at the source of the Onon River sees him formally adopt the title Genghis Khan
The Jin capital Zhongdu surrenders after a four-year campaign and is sacked
He invades the Khwarazmian Empire after the killing of his envoy
He dies in August while subduing the Western Xia, whose capital falls the following month

sections.early:
Genghis Khan was born Temüjin, the eldest child of Yesügei, a chieftain of the Borjigin clan of the Mongol tribe, and of his principal wife Hö'elün, originally of the Olkhonud clan, whom Yesügei had abducted from her Merkit bridegroom. The year of his birth is disputed: historians favour 1155, 1162 or 1167, and 1162 is the date accepted by most; the historian Paul Ratchnevsky noted that Temüjin himself may not have known the truth. The Secret History of the Mongols records the birthplace as Delüün Boldog on the Onon River.

All accounts of his youth derive from two Mongolian sources, the Secret History and the lost Altan Debter. When Temüjin was eight his father betrothed him to Börte, daughter of the Onggirat chieftain Dei Sechen, and left him in her father's household. Riding home, Yesügei asked a meal of a band of Tatars, who recognised their old enemy and poisoned his food; he died soon after. Most of his people then renounced the family in favour of the Tayichiud clan, and Hö'elün and her children were reduced to gathering roots and nuts, hunting small animals and fishing.

As the children grew, Temüjin and his elder half-brother Behter both had claims to be their father's heir, and Temüjin and his younger brother Qasar ambushed and killed Behter, a taboo act omitted from the official chronicles but recounted in the Secret History. Around this time he swore the anda pact, the oath of blood brothers, with Jamukha. Captured by the Tayichiuds, he escaped during a feast with the help of Sorkan-Shira, who sheltered him for three days.
sections.rise:
At fifteen Temüjin returned to marry Börte. He won the protection of Toghrul, khan of the Kerait tribe and his father's sworn brother. When around 300 Merkits raided his camp and abducted Börte, Toghrul and Jamukha fielded armies to recover her; she soon gave birth to a son, Jochi, whose paternity was questioned throughout his life. Temüjin and Jamukha later parted; forty-one leaders and many commoners followed Temüjin, who was soon acclaimed khan of the Mongols by his close followers.

In around 1187 the two clashed at Dalan Baljut, where Temüjin suffered a clear defeat. Historians such as Ratchnevsky and Timothy May consider it very likely that he spent much of the following decade as a servant of the Jurchen Jin dynasty in North China. In 1196 he joined a Jin campaign against the Tatars and helped Toghrul to reclaim the lordship of the Kereit. Around 1201 he and Toghrul routed a confederation that had elected Jamukha its leader; Temüjin then defeated the Tayichiud and, in 1202, the Tatars, executing the clan leaders and taking the remaining warriors into his service.

In 1203 Toghrul turned on his vassal, and Temüjin was soundly defeated at the Battle of Qalaqaljid Sands. He retreated to Baljuna, where he swore an oath of loyalty with followers from nine tribes, then ambushed the Kereit at the Jej'er Heights and won a three-day battle. In May 1204 he defeated the Naimans at the Battle of Chakirmaut. Jamukha was betrayed to him and put to death, honourably and at his own request according to the Secret History, by dismemberment in other accounts.
sections.deeds:
At a kurultai, a large assembly, held at the source of the Onon River in 1206, Temüjin formally adopted the title Genghis Khan, whose meaning is debated. He then began what May calls a "social revolution". Every man between fifteen and seventy was conscripted into a minqan, a unit of a thousand, and the warriors of defeated tribes were dispersed among the units so that old tribal identities would give way to loyalty to the khan and his family. Commands went to companions chosen for merit, and the keshig, the bodyguard, was expanded from 1,150 to 10,000 men.

In 1209 he led a full-scale invasion of the Tangut-led Western Xia, whose emperor submitted and handed over tribute after the Mongols withdrew in 1210. In 1211 he invaded the Jin; after a peace in 1214 and the Jin court's move south to Kaifeng he returned, and Zhongdu (modern-day Beijing) surrendered on 31 May 1215 and was sacked. His general Jebe annexed the Central Asian state of Qara Khitai in 1218.

After the governor of Otrar massacred a caravan of 450 merchants in 1218 and the Khwarazmian ruler Muhammad II killed a Mongol ambassador, Genghis invaded the Khwarazmian Empire. Otrar was besieged from autumn 1219 and fell in February 1220, Bukhara's citadel the same month and Samarkand the next; Gurganj fell in spring 1221, and the prince Jalal al-Din was beaten at the Battle of the Indus in November 1221. Jebe and Subutai pursued Muhammad until his death and went on to a 7,500-kilometre expedition around the Caspian Sea that brought the Mongols into contact with Europe for the first time.
sections.opponents:
Genghis faced rivals inside as well as outside his following. Jamukha drew attention to the threat he posed to the traditional steppe aristocracy by promoting commoners to high positions. The shaman Kokechu, called Teb Tenggeri, who had proclaimed him Genghis Khan, sought to divide the imperial family and humiliated his brothers Qasar and Temüge; warned by Börte, Genghis allowed Temüge to arrange the shaman's death and took his place as the Mongols' highest spiritual authority.

In Khorasan his son Tolui destroyed every city that resisted; Nishapur, Merv and Herat, three of the largest and wealthiest cities in the world, were annihilated. Contemporary Persian historians put the dead of those three sieges alone at over 5.7 million, a number modern scholars regard as grossly exaggerated, though even the 1.25 million estimated by John Man for the whole campaign would have been a demographic catastrophe. The Persian chronicler Juzjani, an eyewitness to the conquests, wrote with hostility; Juvayni, who served a Mongol successor state, was more sympathetic. When the Xia capital fell in 1227 its population was treated with extreme savagery, in what Man described as a "very successful ethnocide".

Genghis believed that the supreme deity Tengri had destined him for world power, and anyone who did not recognise that right was treated as an enemy. He is remembered as a backward, savage tyrant in Russia and the Arab world, where he is perceived as the "accursed enemy". Perhaps his greatest failing was his inability to create a working succession system.
sections.last:
Genghis halted his Central Asian campaigns in 1221 and, after much of 1222 was spent overcoming rebellions in Khorasan, withdrew to a new frontier on the Amu Darya river. On the way home he summoned the Taoist patriarch Changchun to the Hindu Kush. He returned to Mongolia in early 1225 and prepared a campaign against the Western Xia, who had declined to provide auxiliaries in 1219. It began in the first months of 1226; the cities of the Gansu Corridor were sacked one by one, and on 4 December he defeated a Xia relief army.

He fell from his horse while hunting in the winter of 1226–1227 and grew increasingly ill. He died on either 18 or 25 August 1227; the death was kept secret, and the Xia capital Zhongxing fell the following month. Rashid al-Din and the History of Yuan mention an illness, possibly malaria, typhus or bubonic plague; Marco Polo claimed that he was shot by an arrow, and Carpini that he was struck by lightning. He was buried on or near the sacred Burkhan Khaldun peak in the Khentii Mountains.

He had recognised his third son, Ögedei, as heir, in 1219 according to the Secret History or before the final Xia campaign according to Rashid al-Din. Jochi, from whom he had become estranged, had died of an illness; Chagatai was thought uncompromising; Tolui was the better commander, but Ögedei was generous and generally well liked. Tolui served as regent and, persuaded by the adviser Yelü Chucai, held the kurultai that crowned Ögedei in 1229, when the grave was honoured with three days of offerings and the sacrifice of thirty maidens.
sections.legacy:
Genghis Khan founded the largest contiguous state in world history, which, according to the historian Christopher Atwood, permanently altered the worldview of European, Islamic and East Asian civilizations. His conquests enabled Eurasian trading systems unprecedented in scale, and he reorganised the legal system under a judicial authority headed by Shigi Qutuqu, though he very likely did not codify the body of laws known as the Great Yasa. His division of it into appanages, however, led it to begin splitting in the late 1200s into the Golden Horde, the Chagatai Khanate, the Ilkhanate and the Yuan dynasty, established by his grandson Kublai Khan in 1271.

In post-Mongol Asia descent from him was a source of legitimacy: Timur ruled behind puppet khans of his line. In Mongolia he was deified after Altan Khan's conversion to Tibetan Buddhism in the late 1500s, and in the 19th and early 20th century came to be seen as the national hero. After the Second World War his cult was repressed and celebrations of the 800th anniversary of his birth in 1962 were cancelled after Soviet threats; since the 1990 revolution he has been rehabilitated, and he is generally recognised as the founding father of Mongolia.

Russian historians have portrayed the rule of the Golden Horde as backward and destructive; modern Chinese historiography has generally viewed him positively. In the West he was seen in the 14th century as a just and wise ruler and by the twentieth as a barbarian warlord; recent scholarship views him as a more complex individual.

summary: Genghis Khan (born Temüjin; c. 1162 – 1227) united the tribes of the Mongolian steppe and in 1206 founded the Mongol Empire. His campaigns against the Western Xia, the Jin and the Khwarazmian Empire killed millions and opened exchange across Eurasia; he remains a controversial figure, the founding father of Mongolia and a tyrant in other memories.
references: Christopher P. Atwood, Encyclopedia of Mongolia and the Mongol Empire (Facts on File, 2004)
Vasily Barthold, Turkestan Down To The Mongol Invasion (Munshiram Manoharlal, 1992)
John Andrew Boyle, The Cambridge History of Iran Volume 5: The Saljuq and Mongol Periods (Cambridge University Press, 1968)
Anne F. Broadbridge, Women and the Making of the Mongol Empire (Cambridge University Press, 2018)
